description:
We are "CIS Galaxy Express", students passionate about space history. We are tackling the "Abandoned but not Forgotten" challenge to turn the history of NASA's equipment left on the Moon and Mars into fun stories for kids.
We need teammates with:
Research skills: To gather historical facts about NASA's hardware.
Writing/Storytelling: To simplify science for children.
Design skills: To create visual storybooks.
Join us to bring space history to life!
summary:
Twin Rover Quest is a story-game website that tells children under 10 the true story of Spirit and Opportunity, the twin NASA rovers left on Mars. Built for a 90-day mission, Spirit kept working for more than six years and Opportunity for more than fourteen. Both are still on Mars today, silent.

Children meet the twins and tap their parts to learn what each one did. Then they play through the rovers’ journey on a Mission Map of five levels and a finale. Each level links one engineering part to one real discovery: the airbag landing, the broken wheel that found silica, winter on Low Ridge, Opportunity’s “blueberries” and the dust storm. Players earn badges, ask the rovers questions in a helper that answers only from NASA facts, and end by reading each robot’s imagined letter.

Every fact links to its NASA source, and imagined voices are clearly labelled. Level 1 is fully playable in our prototype.

This answers the challenge by turning “abandoned” machines into heroes a new generation will remember, while teaching real planetary science through play.
details:
Twin Rover Quest is a story-game website that tells children under 10 the true story of Spirit and Opportunity, the twin NASA rovers left on Mars. A child moves through the twins’ journey in 15 to 20 minutes:

  1. Meet the Twins: tap five parts on a cartoon rover (wheels, camera mast, arm, solar panels, antenna) to learn what each does and which discovery it led to.
  2. Mission Map: a trail of five levels and a finale. Each level links one engineering part to one real discovery: the airbag landing, the broken wheel that dug up silica, surviving winter on Low Ridge, Opportunity’s “blueberries” and salty sea, and the 2018 dust storm.
  3. Badges: each level earns a badge and unlocks a page of a printed cartoon book with QR codes that open the level.
  4. Ask the Rover: a helper that answers in Spirit’s or Oppy’s voice, only from facts checked on NASA pages, with a source on every answer.
  5. Letters from Mars: each robot’s imagined letter, plus a status card saying where it is today.

Level 1, Crash Landing, is fully playable. The child taps PARACHUTE, AIRBAGS, ROCKETS and CUT at the right moment, then counts the bounces. Levels 2 to 5 are designed as concept screens.

Benefits and intended impact

Children learn real planetary science by playing a story, not by memorizing facts. Parents and teachers get a free activity where every fact links to its NASA source. Two “abandoned” machines become heroes a new generation remembers. We hope this method can tell the stories of other equipment left on the Moon and Mars.

Tools and technology

  • HTML, CSS and JavaScript in one self-contained page, hosted on GitHub Pages
  • Hand-drawn SVG cartoons and our own line icons
  • Web Audio for sound, off by default
  • Browser local storage for progress, with no accounts
  • Fredoka and Nunito fonts
  • NASA Photojournal images, JPL mission pages and NASA technical papers as our sources
  • AI: Claude (Anthropic) helped improve the website design and draft our documentation and presentation. All facts were checked by the team.

Creativity

Instead of a fact sheet, we told the rovers’ story as a game with a beginning, a problem and an ending. Each level teaches one part and one discovery through play. Robot voices, speech bubbles and letters make children care, and the printed QR book moves the story from paper to screen.

Factors we considered

  • Honesty: imagined voices are always labelled. Every fact sits in a “NASA fact” box with its source. We never call the rovers “dead” or “junk”, and we never say they found life.
  • Age: short sentences, big buttons, no timers and no game-over screen. Auto-pilot helps after two misses.
  • Accessibility: sound is off by default and every sound has a caption. Slow motion and keyboard play are included.
  • Privacy: no names, no accounts and no data collected. Ask the Rover keeps nothing after it closes.
  • Transparency: every part is labelled as working or concept, so judges see what really exists.
